identification.summary: GCMAN is a financially motivated criminal group publicly named by Kaspersky Lab in February 2016, alongside Metel and Carbanak 2.0, for APT-style intrusions into banks [S1][S2]. MITRE describes it as a group that targets banks to transfer money to e-currency services [S5]. Kaspersky says the name comes from the group's use of the GCC compiler, which is rare among malware writers [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly disclosed by Kaspersky on 2016-02-08 [S2]. ETDA lists first seen as 2016 [S6]. Kaspersky's earliest intrusion date is not established in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Kaspersky says there is no direct connection between the Carbanak, Metel and GCMAN attacks; Golovanov called Metel and GCMAN copycats of Carbanak in some respects [S2]. Keep the three clusters separate. No Microsoft naming applies; Microsoft does not appear to track this actor under a weather-based name in the sources gathered. No aliases are stated by a cited source.

attribution.confidence: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered. ETDA classifies the motivation as financial crime [S6]. Kaspersky found victims only in Russia and suspected the activity is more widespread [S3][S2]; this is a victimology statement, not an attribution of origin.
attribution.basis: Kaspersky Lab incident-response and analysis reporting [S1][S2]; MITRE ATT&CK summary of Kaspersky reporting [S5]. The country code RU in this encyclopedia's imported record is not supported by a cited statement of actor origin and should not be treated as attribution.

objectives: Direct financial theft: moving money out of bank systems to multiple e-currency services [S5][S3].

regions: Russia (the only victims Kaspersky identified; three financial institutions per press coverage) [S3]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky said it suspects infection is much more widespread than the Russian victims it identified [S3][S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access by spear-phishing a financial institution with a malicious RAR archive that launches an executable instead of the Word document it imitates [S2][S6]. Lateral movement with legitimate and penetration-testing tools including PuTTY, VNC and Meterpreter [S3][S6]. The group located servers handling financial transactions and set up cron jobs to automate transfers to multiple e-currency services, mostly on weekends; Secondary reporting of Kaspersky's findings cites a cron script generating transactions at about $200 per minute [S3]. Press coverage of Kaspersky's findings reports the group waited about a year and a half after initial compromise before taking money in one incident [S3]. Malware was built with the GCC compiler [S2]. MITRE lists PuTTY and VNC use for lateral movement [S5].

campaigns.name: Kaspersky public disclosure of GCMAN with Metel and Carbanak 2.0
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reports GCMAN bank intrusions with automated cron-driven transfers to e-currency services, with victims identified only in Russia, and publishes indicators of compromise.

campaigns.name: Long-dwell bank intrusion with delayed cash-out
campaigns.summary: In one incident reported in press coverage of Kaspersky research, about 18 months passed between initial compromise and the start of money theft; the incident date and victim are not given in the sources gathered.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated criminal group named GCMAN by Kaspersky; individual identities, affiliation and origin not established [S1][S6].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with malicious RAR archive, PuTTY, VNC, Meterpreter, GCC-compiled malware, cron-scheduled automated transfers [S3][S6][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Not described in the cited material available to me; Kaspersky published IOCs that I could not open [S2].
diamond.victim: Banks and financial institutions; Russian victims identified [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit motive. Kaspersky frames the group as part of a trend of criminals adopting APT-style methods against banks [S2].
diamond.technology: Bank servers that handle financial transactions and the ability to push transfers to e-currency services without relying on malware on endpoints; use of scheduled jobs on servers [S3].

gaps: Could not open the primary Securelist report, the MITRE page, PCWorld or ETDA directly (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries of those pages and Kaspersky's press release coverage. Validate against the Securelist report [S1].
Exact dates, victims and loss totals of GCMAN intrusions are not established; the 18-month dwell time appears only in press coverage [S3].
Actor origin, membership, and any link to Carbanak or Metel are unknown; Kaspersky states no direct connection [S2].
Infrastructure, malware hashes and IOCs were published by Kaspersky but not reviewed here [S2].
Whether the group remains active after 2016 is unverified; a third-party summary suggests Securelist lists it as inactive since 2017, which I could not confirm.
Some secondary Q&A sites add details (log deletion, specific payment services, ATT&CK mappings beyond PuTTY/VNC) that I did not rely on.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the bank server tier that originates or relays payment transactions, plus staff mailboxes. The group is a criminal actor, so relevance to DoD is mainly via financial-sector disruption and partner-nation banking, not direct DoD networks. STEP 2: Environment features include weak monitoring of scheduled jobs on transaction servers and reliance on legitimate admin tools that blend in. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish with RAR, long dwell with PuTTY/VNC/Meterpreter, then cron-scheduled transfers to e-currency services, favoring weekends [S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume automated theft from banks. MDCOA is use of the same access methods against financial entities supporting military pay or logistics. Candidate indicators: new cron entries on transaction servers, RAR attachments launching executables, unexpected PuTTY/VNC on servers, and weekend transaction bursts [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: financial-sector criminal reporting is a low-priority feed unless military-affiliated financial systems are affected. (2) Authorities: this is a criminal matter, so response runs through law enforcement and financial regulators rather than offensive or defensive cyber operations authorities. (3) Mission assurance: protect payment and pay-system servers with monitoring of scheduled tasks and remote-admin tools. (4) Coordination: share indicators through established sector and DC3 channels where DoD-linked financial services are involved.
